title: For the Sake of Their House
bodyHtml:
The Permyak language is spoken by around 60,000 people on the western slope of the Ural Mountains in Russia. It belongs to the Finno-Ugric language family, along with Finnish, Estonian, Hungarian, and other languages that are mostly spoken in Russia.

Examine the following words in Permyak and their translations in English:

PermyakEnglish
1.cerkulaɲtowards the house
2.pɨzannezɨtlənof your (sg.) desks
3.ponɨtyour (sg.) dog
4.purtnɨstheir knife
5.kəinnezɨshis wolves
6.vərələnof my forest
7.purtəlafor the sake of my knife
8.tɨezɨtkətwith your (sg.) lakes
9.cerkuezliɕfrom the houses
10.juɕɕezəmy swans
11.kokɨskətwith his foot
12.ciɨtlaɲtowards your (sg.) hand

Notes: ɨ and ə are special vowel sounds of Permyak; c, ɕ, and ɲ are pronounced similarly to k, s, and n, respectively. The abbreviations sg. and pl. stand for singular and plural. The word their has a plural meaning rather than a gender-neutral singular meaning.

questions.partPrompt: Translate the following Permyak words into English.

questions.answerKey: for the sake of the swan
acceptedVariants: for the sake of a swan

questions.partPrompt: Translate the following English phrases into Permyak.

questions.promptHtml: d. for the sake of their house

hints.text: Every Permyak word here is one root followed by a string of endings. Line up words that share a beginning, like cerkulaɲ "towards the house" and cerkuezliɕ "from the houses", to peel the endings off one at a time.

The endings always come in the same order: root, then plural, then possessor ("my", "your", "his", "their"), then case ("of", "towards", "with", "from", "for the sake of"). Watch what happens to the consonant at the end of a root when the plural ending is added.

Try kəinnezɨs "his wolves". Item 5 is the only wolf word, but compare it with juɕɕezə "my swans": both plurals contain ez, and in both the consonant just before it is doubled. So kəinnezɨs splits as kəin (wolf) + n-ez (plural) + ɨs (his). Now check that ɨs really means "his" against item 11.

explanationHtml:
What kind of puzzle is this?

Every Permyak word in the list is a single noun carrying a chain of endings (suffixes). Our job is to find where each ending starts and stops, and what each one means. This is called morphological analysis: cutting words into meaningful pieces (morphemes).

Step 1: find the roots

Look for English glosses that share a noun and Permyak words that share a beginning. "Towards the house" is cerkulaɲ and "from the houses" is cerkuezliɕ: both start with cerku, so cerku = "house". Doing the same across the list gives:

cerku
house
pɨzan
desk
pon
dog
purt
knife
tɨ
lake
vər
forest
kəin
wolf
juɕ
swan
kok
foot
ci
hand

Step 2: find the case endings (the last piece)

The last chunk of each word matches the English preposition:

-lən
of
-laɲ
towards
-la
for the sake of
-liɕ
from
-kət
with

Check: vərələn "of my forest" is vər + something + lən, and purtəla "for the sake of my knife" is purt + the same something + la. That leftover ə must mean "my".

Step 3: the possessive endings

Comparing more words gives the possessors, which sit right before the case ending:

-ə
my
-ɨt
your (sg.)
-ɨs
his
-nɨs
their

Notice the neat pattern: the plural possessor "their" is just "his" with an extra n in front. So "your (pl.)" should be "your (sg.)" with the same extra n: -nɨt. Item 3 confirms it in reverse: ponɨt is "your (sg.) dog", so ponnɨt (with an extra n that cannot be a plural marker, since there is no ez) has to mean "your (pl.) dog".

Step 4: the plural, and the doubling trick

The plural marker is -ez, and it goes immediately after the root: cerku-ez-liɕ "from the houses". But look at juɕɕezə "my swans" from root juɕ, and pɨzannezɨtlən "of your (sg.) desks" from root pɨzan. When the root ends in a consonant, that consonant is doubled before -ez. After a vowel (cerku, tɨ) nothing is doubled.

The whole template

root + (plural) + (possessive) + (case). Now the answers fall out.

D1: Permyak into English

  • pɨzanɨsliɕ = pɨzan (desk) + ɨs (his) + liɕ (from). No ez, so singular: "from his desk".
  • vərrezlən = vər + doubled r + ez (plural) + lən (of). No possessor: "of the forests".
  • ponnɨt = pon + nɨt (your pl.): "your (pl.) dog".
  • juɕla = juɕ (swan) + la: "for the sake of the swan".

D2: English into Permyak

  • his hands = ci + ez (plural, no doubling after a vowel) + ɨs = ciezɨs.
  • my dogs = pon + doubled n + ez + ə = ponnezə.
  • of your (pl.) feet = kok + doubled k + ez + nɨt + lən = kokkeznɨtlən.
  • for the sake of their house = cerku + "their" + la = cerkunɨla (the official key).

That last one is worth a comment: from the pattern you would expect cerkunɨsla, since "their" is -nɨs. The official answer key drops the s, which suggests the s is lost before the case ending -la. If you wrote the fully regular form, you reasoned correctly, and it is accepted here too.
